events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 909, Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah ascended as the leader of the Fatimid state, declaring himself Caliph Abdullah (al-Mahdi). His proclamation marked the establishment of the Fatimid Caliphate, which would play a crucial role in Islamic history and politics.
events.name: Winter – Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah takes up the leadership of the Fatimid state and proclaims himself Caliph Abdullah (al-Mahdi)

events.enhanced_description: In 909, the Min Kingdom was established in modern-day Fujian province by governor Wang Shenzhi, who sought to create an efficient bureaucracy and tax system. Fuzhou, known as Changle, became the capital, marking a significant development in regional governance and culture.
events.name: The Min Kingdom is established by governor Wang Shenzhi

events.enhanced_description: In 909, the Battle of Jisu took place between the warlord brothers Liu Shouguang and Liu Shouwen, culminating in Liu Shouguang's victory. This conflict was part of the larger power struggles during the tumultuous period of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms in China.
events.name: Battle of Jisu - the warlord brothers Liu Shouguang and Liu Shouwen fight

events.enhanced_description: In 909, the last Long Count date was inscribed on a monument at the Mayan site of Toniná in present-day Chiapas, Mexico. This inscription marked the end of the Classic Maya Period, signifying a pivotal transition in Maya civilization.
events.name: The last Long Count date is inscribed at Toniná

events.enhanced_description: In 909, Asser, the bishop of Sherborne, passed away, leading to significant ecclesiastical changes as his See was divided. This event resulted in the creation of new bishoprics at Wells, Crediton, Ramsbury, and Sonning, reshaping the religious landscape of the region.
events.name: Asser, bishop of Sherborne, dies

events.enhanced_description: In 910, the Battle of Rednitz resulted in a significant victory for the Hungarians against the East Frankish army near the Rednitz River, leading to the death of Gebhard, Duke of Lotharingia. This defeat forced King Louis IV to agree to pay tribute to the Hungarian state, altering the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Rednitz: The Hungarians defeat the East Frankish army

events.enhanced_description: In 910, the Battle of Tettenhall marked a decisive confrontation where King Edward the Elder attacked the joint-Kings Eowils and Halfdan of Norse York. The battle resulted in the deaths of all three Viking monarchs, significantly weakening Norse power in England.
events.name: Battle of Tettenhall: King Edward the Elder attacks the joint-Kings Eowils and Halfdan

events.enhanced_description: In 910, William I (the Pious) of Aquitaine donated land in Burgundy for the establishment of a Benedictine monastery dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul, which would become the Abbey of Cluny. This act not only marked a significant moment in monastic history but also placed the abbey directly under papal authority.
events.name: William I of Aquitaine donates land for a Benedictine monastery

events.enhanced_description: In 910, Gabriel I was appointed as Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church in Alexandria, succeeding his predecessor. His leadership would influence the Coptic community during a period of significant religious and political challenges.
events.name: Gabriel I becomes Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church

events.enhanced_description: Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, died after a tumultuous reign that saw the division of the united monarchy into the northern Kingdom of Israel and the southern Kingdom of Judah. His leadership was marked by heavy taxation and the eventual rebellion of the northern tribes.
events.name: Death of Rehoboam, King of Judah

events.enhanced_description: Adad-nirari II ascended to the throne of Assyria following the death of his father, Ashur-Dan II. His reign marked a significant period of expansion and consolidation for the Assyrian Empire, strengthening its military and administrative capabilities.

image.caption: Inscribed stone tablet of Adad-nirari II with a cuneiform inscription about his construction work.
image.credit: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg) — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image was photographed on 2019-03-14; the tablet is identified as belonging to Adad-nirari II’s reign (912–891 BCE). It is not a depiction of the succession event itself.

events.name: Adad-nirari II Succeeds Ashur-Dan II as King of Assyria

events.enhanced_description: Abijah, the King of Judah, died after a reign marked by conflicts with the northern kingdom of Israel. His death led to a succession crisis and the eventual takeover by his son Asa, who would continue the religious reforms initiated by his father.
events.name: Death of Abijah, King of Judah

events.enhanced_description: Nadab became king of Israel after the death of his father Jeroboam I around 910 BCE. His reign was marked by continued conflict with the Kingdom of Judah and the challenges of maintaining the integrity of the northern kingdom.
events.name: Nadab Succeeds Jeroboam I as King of Israel

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 910, King Alfonso III of Asturias was compelled to abdicate, partitioning his kingdom among his three sons. García I became king of León, Ordoño II ruled Galicia, and Fruela II received Asturias, leading to a significant reorganization of power in the region.
events.name: Summer – King Alfonso III of Asturias abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: In 910, the Battle of Augsburg saw the Hungarians decisively defeat the East Frankish army led by the young King Louis IV, utilizing their renowned feigned retreat tactic. Count Gausbert, the actual commander, was killed in the battle, highlighting the vulnerabilities of the East Frankish forces.
events.name: Battle of Augsburg: The Hungarians defeat the East Frankish army

events.enhanced_description: In 911, King Louis IV (the Child), the last Carolingian ruler of the East Frankish Kingdom, died in Frankfurt am Main after an 11-year reign. His death led to the election of Conrad I as king, marking a significant transition in the leadership of the East Frankish Kingdom.
events.name: King Louis IV (the Child) dies at Frankfurt am Main

events.enhanced_description: In 911, the Hungarians launched an invasion across Bavaria, plundering territories in Swabia and Franconia. This incursion marked a significant moment in the conflicts between the Hungarians and the various Germanic states.
events.name: The Hungarians invade Swabia and Franconia

events.enhanced_description: In 911, the Fatimids initiated their conquest of Sicily, challenging the Aghlabid rule. Under the leadership of governor Ibn al-Khinzir, this campaign marked the beginning of significant Islamic influence in the region.
events.name: The Fatimids begin the conquest of Sicily

events.enhanced_description: In 911, Lord Æthelred of Mercia passed away, leading to his wife, Princess Æthelflæd, succeeding him as Lady of the Mercians. This transition marked an important moment in the governance of Mercia during a time of Viking incursions.
events.name: Lord Æthelred of Mercia dies

events.enhanced_description: In 911, a rebellion erupted among the Kutama Berbers against the Fatimid Caliphate, a significant shift given that the Kutama had been key supporters of the Shia regime. This uprising reflected the growing tensions within the region.
events.name: A rebellion of the Kutama Berbers against the Fatimid Caliphate occurs

events.enhanced_description: In 911, Pope Sergius III died after a seven-year reign, leading to the election of Anastasius III as his successor. This change in papal leadership would influence the direction of the Catholic Church during a turbulent period.
events.name: Pope Sergius III dies at Rome

events.enhanced_description: Nadab ascended to the throne of Israel following the death of his father, Jeroboam I, after a reign of 22 years. His reign marked a continuation of the policies established by his father, although it was short-lived due to political instability.
events.name: Nadab becomes King of Israel

events.enhanced_description: In the autumn of 911, King Charles III (the Simple) and Rollo, the Viking leader, signed the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, establishing a peace agreement. This treaty marked the beginning of the Duchy of Normandy, as Rollo became a vassal in exchange for his conversion to Christianity.
events.name: Autumn – King Charles III and Rollo sign a peace agreement

events.enhanced_description: In 912, Emperor Leo VI (the Wise) passed away after a 26-year reign during which he completed the Byzantine code of laws known as the Basilika. His death led to the ascension of his brother Alexander III and his young son Constantine VII, marking a significant transition in Byzantine leadership.
events.name: Emperor Leo VI dies after a 26-year reign

events.enhanced_description: In 912, German dukes Henry the Fowler of Saxony and Arnulf I (the Bad) of Bavaria declared themselves sovereign princes, rejecting the authority of King Conrad I of the East Frankish Kingdom. This assertion of independence highlighted the political fragmentation of the region during this period.
events.name: German dukes claim sovereignty against King Conrad I

events.enhanced_description: In 912, Orso II Participazio was elected as the doge of Venice, a pivotal role in the governance of the city-state. His leadership included diplomatic efforts, such as sending his son to Constantinople to strengthen ties with the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Orso II Participazio becomes the doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 912, King Ordoño II of Galicia continued his expansionist policies, sacking the cities of Mérida and Évora. This military campaign was part of the broader Christian reconquest efforts during the early medieval period.
events.name: King Ordoño II of Galicia expands his territory

events.enhanced_description: In 912, Lady Æthelflæd of Mercia undertook significant military fortifications by constructing defensive burghs at Shrewsbury and Bridgnorth. These fortifications were essential for protecting Mercia against Viking raids from the Danelaw.
events.name: Lady Æthelflæd builds defensive burghs

events.enhanced_description: In 912, Abd al-Rahman III succeeded his grandfather Abdullah ibn Muhammad as emir of Córdoba after the latter's execution. His ascension marked the beginning of a powerful and influential period in Al-Andalus, shaping the Islamic presence in the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Abd al-Rahman III becomes emir of Córdoba

events.enhanced_description: The Kutama tribesmen, dissatisfied with the Fatimid Caliphate's rule, rise in rebellion for the second time within two years, reflecting the ongoing tensions and resistance against the caliphate's authority in North Africa.
events.name: The second rebellion in two years, of the Kutama tribesmen against the Fatimid Caliphate, occurs

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Taizu, also known as Zhu Wen, is assassinated by his eldest son Zhu Yougui in the imperial palace at Kaifeng, marking a significant power shift in the Later Liang dynasty after a brief five-year reign.
events.name: Emperor Taizu (Zhu Wen) is murdered in the imperial palace at Kaifeng

events.enhanced_description: In a significant ecclesiastical shift, Euthymius I is deposed as Patriarch of Constantinople, paving the way for the restoration of Nicholas Mystikos, reflecting the ongoing political and religious tensions within the Byzantine Church.
events.name: Euthymius I is deposed as Patriarch of Constantinople, and Nicholas Mystikos is restored

events.enhanced_description: Adad-nirari II succeeded his father Ashur-Dan II as king of Assyria, continuing the legacy of military expansion and consolidation of power in the region. His reign is noted for significant military campaigns that strengthened Assyrian dominance.
events.name: Adad-nirari II becomes King of Assyria

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Alexander III dies of exhaustion while playing tzykanion, a game similar to polo, leading to the ascension of his young nephew Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, with a regency council managing the empire during his minority.
events.name: Emperor Alexander III dies of exhaustion while playing the game tzykanion

events.enhanced_description: In August, during the Byzantine–Bulgarian War, Simeon I leads a large Bulgarian army to Constantinople, besieging the city and ultimately negotiating recognition as emperor of the Bulgarians, showcasing the rising power of Bulgaria.
events.name: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Simeon I launches a campaign

events.enhanced_description: In a failed coup, Byzantine general Constantine Doukas attempts to usurp the throne from the young Constantine VII but is killed in the ensuing conflict, demonstrating the political instability of the era.
events.name: Constantine Doukas attempts to usurp the throne from Constantine VII

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Inn sees Hungarian forces invading Bavaria, Swabia, and Northern Burgundy, only to be defeated by a coalition of local dukes at Aschbach, highlighting the ongoing conflicts in Central Europe.
events.name: Battle of the Inn: The Hungarians invade Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: King Edward the Elder initiates the reconquest of the Danelaw by occupying Essex, following the death of High-Reeve Eadwulf II, which sets the stage for ongoing conflicts with Norse forces in the region.
events.name: King Edward the Elder begins the 'reconquest' of the Danelaw

events.enhanced_description: Caliph Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah of the Fatimid Caliphate replaces the unpopular governor Ibn Abi Khinzir with Ali ibn Umar al-Balawi, leading to unrest in Sicily as local lords declare independence and seek allegiance with the Abbasid Caliphate.
events.name: Caliph Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah replaces governor Ibn Abi Khinzir

events.enhanced_description: Pope Anastasius III dies after a brief two-year reign, leading to the election of Lando as his successor, a transition that reflects the ongoing power struggles within the papacy.
events.name: Pope Anastasius III dies at Rome

events.enhanced_description: San Miguel de Escalada is constructed in León, Northern Spain, under the orders of King García I, representing a significant development in the architectural landscape of the region during this period.
events.name: San Miguel de Escalada is built in León

events.enhanced_description: In a dramatic palace coup, Empress Zoe Karbonopsina overthrows Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos as regent for her son, Emperor Constantine VII, asserting her influence in Byzantine politics.
events.name: Empress Zoe Karbonopsina leads a palace coup at Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: During the summer, Simeon I leads a Bulgarian invasion into the Byzantine themes of Thrace and Macedonia, capturing Adrianople but later relinquishing it for a hefty ransom, illustrating the volatile nature of regional power dynamics.
events.name: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Simeon I invades Thrace and Macedonia

events.enhanced_description: King García I of León dies in Zamora after a four-year reign, succeeded by his brother Ordoño II, who continues the expansionist policies of their dynasty in Galicia and León.
events.name: King García I dies at Zamora

events.enhanced_description: Saracens from Garigliano establish advanced strongholds in Lazio, encroaching on papal territories and threatening the stability of the region, marking a significant phase of Muslim incursions into Italy.
events.name: Saracens establish strongholds in Lazio

events.enhanced_description: Viking raiders, led by Ottir (the Black), establish a settlement near Waterford, asserting their influence in Ireland while facing tribute demands from local Irish kings, highlighting the complex interactions between Vikings and native populations.
events.name: Viking raiders establish a settlement near Waterford

events.enhanced_description: A severe drought in Al-Andalus leads to a devastating famine across the Iberian Peninsula, prompting the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Rahman III to intensify his centralization efforts by reconquering Seville.
events.name: Drought leads to famine in Al-Andalus

events.enhanced_description: Viking raiders wreak havoc along the Welsh coast and advance up the Severn River, capturing Bishop Cyfeilliog of Ergyng, only to be defeated by local levies, illustrating the ongoing conflict between Viking invaders and the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.
events.name: Vikings devastate the Welsh coast

events.enhanced_description: Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians and daughter of King Alfred the Great, constructs a fortified dwelling at Warwick and repairs Eddisbury hill fort, strengthening defenses against Danish incursions and demonstrating her leadership in the region.
events.name: Æthelflæd builds a burh at Warwick

events.enhanced_description: Fatimid general Hubasa ibn Yusuf leads an invasion into Egypt, capturing key towns along the coastline without resistance, marking a significant expansion of Fatimid influence in North Africa.
events.name: Fatimid general Hubasa ibn Yusuf invades Egypt

events.enhanced_description: Hubasa ibn Yusuf successfully captures Barqah, the ancient capital of Cyrenaica, from the Abbasid governor, significantly boosting the Fatimid's territorial gains and financial resources.
events.name: Hubasa takes Barqah (modern-day Benghazi)

events.enhanced_description: Al-Qa'im bi-Amr Allah, son of the Fatimid caliph, sets out with an army to conquer Egypt, but finds his general Hubasa already advancing independently, showcasing the complexities of military command within the Fatimid hierarchy.
events.name: Al-Qa'im bi-Amr Allah attempts to conquer Egypt

events.enhanced_description: After a victorious encounter near al-Hanniyya, Hubasa captures Alexandria, a pivotal moment in the Fatimid campaign, despite the Abbasid governor's attempts to rally reinforcements.
events.name: Hubasa captures Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: In December, the Fatimid army under Hubasa departs Alexandria, followed by Al-Qa'im bi-Amr Allah, as Abbasid forces prepare a counter-offensive, marking a critical juncture in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: The Fatimid army leaves Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: Ahmad Samani, emir of the Samanid Empire, is assassinated in his tent at Bukhara, leading to a power vacuum filled by his young son Nasr II under regency, amidst attempts by the Abbasids to exploit the ensuing chaos.
events.name: Ahmad Samani is murdered at Bukhara

events.enhanced_description: In 914, Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj led a Muslim army in a campaign against the Georgian principalities, establishing Tiflis as his operational base. His forces demolished the fortifications of Uplistsikhe and captured the fortress of Q'ueli, executing its defender Gobron, marking a significant moment in the region's tumultuous history.
events.name: Sajid invasion of Georgia: A Muslim army under Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj campaigns in the Georgian principalities

events.enhanced_description: In 914, Hasan al-Utrush successfully re-established Zaydid rule over Tabaristan after a prolonged Samanid occupation lasting 14 years. His ascension as emir was accepted by the Zaydid noblemen, solidifying his authority in the region.
events.name: Hasan al-Utrush re-establishes Zaydid rule over the province Tabaristan (Northern Iran)

events.enhanced_description: In 914, the Belanjong pillar was erected on Bali, serving as a significant cultural and historical monument. This event marks an important point in the island's history, reflecting the influence of Indian culture in the region.
events.name: The Belanjong pillar is established on Bali

events.enhanced_description: In 914, Indra III ascended to the throne of the Rashtrakuta Dynasty in India, continuing the legacy of his grandfather, Krishna II. His reign lasted until 929 and was marked by significant political and cultural developments in the region.
events.name: Emperor Indra III of the Rashtrakuta Dynasty begins his rule

events.enhanced_description: In March or April of 914, Pope Lando passed away in Rome after a brief papacy of less than a year. His death led to the election of John X, the archbishop of Ravenna, who became the 122nd pope of the Catholic Church.
events.name: Pope Lando dies at Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 915, Pope John X crowned Berengar I as the Holy Roman Emperor in Rome, a significant event that reinforced Berengar's authority in northern Italy during a time of political fragmentation.
events.name: John X crowns Berengar I as Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1503, the Battle of Garigliano took place near Gaeta, where Spanish forces under Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba defeated a French-Italian mercenary army led by Ludovico II, Marquess of Saluzzo. The battle resulted in significant casualties for the French forces and marked a decisive moment in the Italian Wars.
events.name: Battle of Garigliano

events.enhanced_description: In July 915, the Magyars, led by Zoltán, launched an aggressive campaign into Swabia, Franconia, and Saxony, reaching as far as Bremen, where they burned the city. This invasion marked a significant moment in the Magyar expansion into Central Europe.
events.name: The Magyars attack Swabia, Franconia, and Saxony

events.enhanced_description: In 916, Sicilian Berbers revolted against Emir Ahmed ibn Khorob in Agrigento, ultimately deposing him and offering Sicily to the Fatimid Caliphate. The Caliph welcomed this change but sent an expeditionary force to assert control over the island, leading to Ahmed's execution.
events.name: Sicilian Berbers revolt and depose Emir Ahmed ibn Khorob

events.enhanced_description: In 916, Lady Æthelflæd, daughter of King Alfred the Great, led an army into Brycheiniog to avenge the murder of the Mercian abbot Ecbryht. Her forces captured and burned the royal fort of King Tewdr, taking the queen and others captive.
events.name: Lady Æthelflæd avenges the murder of the Mercian abbot Ecbryht

events.enhanced_description: In 916, Abaoji, the Khitan ruler and founder of the Liao Dynasty, adopted Chinese court formalities, declaring himself emperor and naming his son Yelü Bei as heir apparent. This marked a significant cultural shift and consolidation of power in the region.
events.name: Abaoji declares himself emperor in the Chinese style

events.enhanced_description: In 916, Clement of Ohrid, a prominent Bulgarian scholar and enlightener of the Slavs, passed away. He is remembered as the first bishop of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church and the founder of the first Slavic Literary School, leaving a lasting legacy in Slavic culture.
events.name: Clement of Ohrid dies

events.enhanced_description: In 917, a Byzantine expeditionary force led by General Leo Phokas was decisively defeated by the Bulgarians at the Achelous River. This battle solidified Tsar Simeon I's control over the Balkan Peninsula, except for Constantinople.
events.name: Battle of Achelous

events.enhanced_description: In 917, during the Bulgarian–Serbian War, Simeon I dispatched an expeditionary force to Serbia, where they captured Prince Petar Gojniković. This maneuver effectively established Bulgarian control over Serbia, turning it into a puppet state until 921.
events.name: Bulgarian–Serbian War

events.enhanced_description: In 917, following their attacks in Swabia, the Hungarians sacked and burned Basel, continuing their campaign into Lorraine and Alsace. This invasion led to significant destruction and forced local dukes to pay tribute to the Hungarians.
events.name: Hungarians sack and burn Basel

events.enhanced_description: In 917, the Norse Vikings under Sigtrygg Caech defeated King Augaire mac Ailella of Leinster at the Battle of Confey. This victory allowed Sigtrygg to reclaim Dublin and establish himself as king, while his kinsman returned to England to become King of Northumbria.
events.name: Battle of Confey

events.enhanced_description: In 917, the English army led by Edward the Elder achieved a decisive victory over the Danish Vikings at the Battle of Tempsford. The battle resulted in the death of King Guthrum II and several Danish Jarls, marking a significant moment in the struggle against Viking incursions.
events.name: Battle of Tempsford

events.enhanced_description: In 917, Umayyad forces led by Abi-Abda besieged the repoblación of San Esteban de Gormaz in Northern Spain. However, King Ordoño II of León, with the support of his brother Fruela II of Asturias and Sancho I of Pamplona, successfully defeated the Moors, capturing Abi-Abda and executing him.
events.name: Battle of San Esteban de Gormaz

events.enhanced_description: In 917, Liu Yan, a former governor and military advisor, founded the Great Yue Kingdom, later known as Southern Han, in Panyu, modern Guangdong and Guangxi. He declared himself emperor and sought to strengthen ties with rival states through strategic marriages.
events.name: The Great Yue Kingdom is founded

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 917, Lady Æthelflæd of Mercia forged an alliance with King Constantine II of Scotland against the Norse in York. Her forces captured Derby while her brother, King Edward the Elder, took Towcester, demonstrating the strategic cooperation between the two leaders.
events.name: Lady Æthelflæd of Mercia allies with King Constantine II of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In the fall of 917, the Bulgarian army under Simeon I advanced toward Constantinople, where they encountered the Byzantine forces led by Leo Phokas. The Bulgarians achieved a surprise victory, routing the Byzantines and further asserting their dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Katasyrtai

events.enhanced_description: In 918, King Conrad I died at Weilburg Castle after a seven-year reign, having been injured in battle against Arnulf I. On his deathbed, he persuaded his brother Eberhard III to offer the East Frankish crown to Henry the Fowler, marking a pivotal transition in the region's leadership.
events.name: King Conrad I dies at Weilburg Castle

events.enhanced_description: In 918, High-Reeve Ealdred I allied with King Constantine II of Scotland to reclaim his position in Bernicia. They faced the Vikings under Ragnall ua Ímair at Corbridge, where the Vikings emerged victorious but suffered heavy casualties.
events.name: Battle of Corbridge

events.enhanced_description: In 918, Lady Æthelflæd died at Tamworth while campaigning against the Vikings. She was buried alongside her husband Æthelred in St. Oswald's Priory at Gloucester, leaving a significant legacy in the fight against Viking incursions.
events.name: Æthelflæd dies at Tamworth

events.enhanced_description: In 918, Kings Idwal Foel of Gwynedd and Hywel ap Cadell, along with Prince Clydog of Deheubarth, submitted to the overlordship of Edward the Elder, marking a significant consolidation of power by the Anglo-Saxon king in Wales. This event occurred amidst ongoing Viking raids, particularly on Anglesey, highlighting the turbulent political landscape of the time.
events.name: Kings Idwal Foel of Gwynedd and Hywel ap Cadell, and Prince Clydog of Deheubarth (Wales) submit to the overlordship of Edward the Elder

events.enhanced_description: In 918, Wang Kon, a prominent Korean general, successfully overthrew the short-lived state of Ho Goguryeo and ascended the throne at Cheorwon. This pivotal moment led to the establishment of the Goryeo dynasty, which would play a crucial role in Korean history.
events.name: Wang Kon overthrows Ho Goguryeo and ascends the throne at Cheorwon

events.enhanced_description: In 918, Emperor Taizu of the Khitan Empire occupied the newly fortified city of Shangjing, which translates to 'Supreme Capital.' This strategic move established Shangjing as the residence of the Chinese Liao dynasty, marking a significant expansion of Khitan influence.
events.name: Emperor Taizu of the Khitan Empire occupies Shangjing

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 918, Lady Æthelflæd of Mercia began to intrigue with disaffected factions within the Norse Kingdom of York. Her forces peacefully overran the fortress of Leicester while her brother, King Edward the Elder, took Stamford, showcasing the strategic maneuvering of the Mercian leadership.
events.name: Lady Æthelflæd intrigues with factions in York

events.enhanced_description: In 919, Romanos Lekapenos, the admiral of the Byzantine navy, seized the Boukoleon Palace in Constantinople, effectively consolidating his power. He was named regent for the young Emperor Constantine VII and arranged a marriage between his daughter and the emperor, further solidifying his influence in the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Romanos Lekapenos seizes the Boukoleon Palace

events.enhanced_description: In 919, during the Imperial Diet in Fritzlar, the nobles of Franconia and Saxony elected Henry the Fowler as the ruler of the East Frankish Kingdom. His election marked the beginning of a new era in German history, as he sought to unify the duchies and fortify the realm against external threats.
events.name: Henry the Fowler elected ruler of the East Frankish Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 919, Arnulf, Duke of Bavaria, was elected as anti-king by East Frankish nobles in opposition to Henry I. This political strife coincided with renewed Magyar raids into Bavaria and Northern Italy, leading to significant conflict in the region.
events.name: Arnulf of Bavaria elected as anti-king

events.enhanced_description: In 919, the Battle of Islandbridge saw High King Niall Glándub leading an Irish coalition against the Viking forces of Uí Ímair, commanded by King Sitric Cáech. The battle ended with Niall's death, significantly impacting Irish resistance against Viking incursions.
events.name: Battle of Islandbridge

events.enhanced_description: In 919, Lady Ælfwynn of the Mercians was brought to the court of her uncle, King Edward the Elder, where she was stripped of her authority, marking the end of independent Mercian rule. This event underscored Edward's consolidation of power over the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.
events.name: Lady Ælfwynn is deprived of authority

events.enhanced_description: In 919, Ragnall ua Ímair, a Viking chief from Ireland, seized control of the Norse Kingdom of York, also known as Jórvik, establishing himself as king. This event marked a significant moment in the ongoing Viking influence in England.
events.name: Ragnall ua Ímair takes control of York

events.enhanced_description: In 919, the Fatimid Caliphate of Ifriqiya launched its second invasion of Egypt in an attempt to seize control from the Abbasids. Despite initial advances, the expedition ultimately failed, forcing the Fatimids to retreat.
events.name: Second Fatimid invasion of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of Mara Takla Haymanot in 919, his eldest son Tatadim ascended to the throne as ruler (negus) of the Zagwe Dynasty in Ethiopia. This transition marked a continuation of the Zagwe lineage and its influence in the region.
events.name: Tatadim succeeds Mara Takla Haymanot

events.enhanced_description: In 919, the Battle of Langshan Jiang saw the Wuyue navy, led by Prince Qian Yuanguan, defeat the naval forces of General Peng Yanzhang on the Yangtze River. Utilizing flamethrower ships, the Wuyue forces destroyed a significant portion of the enemy fleet, showcasing innovative military tactics.
events.name: Battle of Langshan Jiang

events.enhanced_description: The Ancestral Puebloans began construction at Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon, New Mexico. This site would become a major center of culture and trade for the Ancestral Puebloans, reflecting their advanced architectural skills.
events.name: Construction at Pueblo Bonito begins

events.enhanced_description: In 919, the Bulgarian Orthodox Church was declared autocephalous and elevated to the rank of patriarchate during an ecclesiastical council. This significant development marked the establishment of an independent Bulgarian religious identity.
events.name: Bulgarian Orthodox Church declared autocephalous

events.enhanced_description: Adad-nirari II ascended to the throne of Assyria following the death of his father, Ashur-Dan II. His reign marked a significant period in Assyrian history, characterized by military campaigns and territorial expansion.
events.name: Adad-nirari II succeeds his father Ashur-Dan II as king of Assyria

events.enhanced_description: The death of Abijah, king of Judah, led to a transition in leadership that would influence the political landscape of the region. His reign was noted for its conflicts with the northern kingdom of Israel.
events.name: Abijah, king of Judah, dies

events.enhanced_description: Nadab succeeded his father Jeroboam I as king of Israel after a reign marked by instability and conflict. His rule was short-lived, reflecting the turbulent political climate of the northern kingdom.
events.name: Nadab, king of Israel succeeds his father Jeroboam I after he reigns of 22 years and dies

events.enhanced_description: In 920, Romanos I crowned himself co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire, sharing the throne with the young Constantine VII. Although Constantine retained his formal title, Romanos effectively became the sole ruler, shaping the future of the empire.
events.name: Romanos I crowned co-emperor of the Byzantine Empire

events.enhanced_description: In 920, the nobles of Lotharingia, led by Gilbert, duke of Lorraine, revolted against King Charles III, recognizing Henry I as their sovereign. This rebellion highlighted the shifting allegiances and political tensions in the region during this period.
events.name: Nobles of Lotharingia revolt against King Charles III

events.enhanced_description: In 920, Henry I successfully conquered Utrecht, which had been under Viking control for 70 years. This victory marked a significant step in consolidating his power in the region and restoring local governance.
events.name: Henry I conquers Utrecht

events.enhanced_description: High-Reeve Ealdred I of the former kingdom of Bernicia and his brother Uhtred submitted to the overlordship of King Edward the Elder. This submission marked a further consolidation of Edward's authority over Northumbria.
events.name: Ealdred I submits to King Edward the Elder

events.enhanced_description: In 920, Hywel Dda, the Welsh ruler, merged the kingdoms of Dyfed and Seisyllwg, establishing a new kingdom known as Deheubarth. This unification was a significant political maneuver that strengthened his rule in Wales.
events.name: Hywel Dda merges Dyfed and Seisyllwg

events.enhanced_description: In 920, at the Battle of Valdejunquera, the Muslim forces of Emir Abd-ar-Rahman III of Córdoba decisively defeated the Christian armies of King Ordoño II of León and King Sancho I of Pamplona. This battle was part of a larger conflict for control over the Iberian Peninsula.
events.name: Battle of Valdejunquera

events.enhanced_description: the Golden Age of the Ghana Empire began, marking a period of prosperity and cultural flourishing in West Africa. This era was characterized by wealth from trade and the development of complex societal structures.
events.name: Golden Age of the Ghana Empire begins

events.enhanced_description: In 920, Emperor Taizu of the Khitan Empire ordered the adoption of a written script, resulting in the creation of the Khitan 'Large Script.' This initiative was part of broader efforts to establish a distinct cultural identity for the Khitan people.
events.name: Emperor Taizu orders adoption of Khitan script

events.enhanced_description: In 920, Muslim chroniclers in Baghdad documented an unusually cold summer, reflecting the climatic variations that could impact agriculture and society. This record highlights the importance of environmental factors in historical narratives.
events.name: Muslim chroniclers record cold summer

events.enhanced_description: The transit of Venus is an astronomical event that occurs when Venus passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, appearing as a small black dot moving across the solar disk. This rare event has been significant in the history of astronomy for measuring the distance from the Earth to the Sun.
events.name: A transit of Venus occurs

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of King Solomon, his son Rehoboam faced challenges in uniting the tribes of Israel, leading to the secession of the northern tribes and the establishment of the kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam. This event marked a significant division in the ancient Hebrew kingdoms.
events.name: Rehoboam's inability to hold the tribes of Israel together after Solomon's death

events.enhanced_description: Shoshenq I, the founder of the 22nd Dynasty of Egypt, led a military campaign into Canaan, asserting Egyptian dominance over the region. This conquest was part of his broader strategy to expand Egypt's influence and secure its borders against rival powers.
events.name: Military conquest of Canaan by Shoshenq I

events.enhanced_description: Osorkon I ascended to the throne of Egypt following the death of his father, Shoshenq I, marking a continuation of the Libyan dynasty that ruled over Egypt during the Third Intermediate Period. His reign is noted for the consolidation of power and the continuation of the traditions established by his father.
events.name: Osorkon I succeeds his father Shoshenq I as king of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: Phorbas served as the Archon of Athens for three decades, during which he played a significant role in the early development of Athenian governance. His death marked a transition in leadership as his son Megacles took over, continuing the lineage of influential political figures in Athens.
events.name: Phorbas, Archon of Athens, dies after a reign of 30 years and is succeeded by his son Megacles

events.enhanced_description: In March 921, Bulgarian forces under kavhan Theodore Sigritsa achieved a significant victory over the Byzantine army at the Battle of Pegae, located near Constantinople. This battle resulted in the devastation of the area and demonstrated the growing power of the Bulgarian state.
events.name: Battle of Pegae

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 921, King Henry I (the Fowler) defeated his rival Arnulf I (the Bad), duke of Bavaria, in two military campaigns. This victory solidified Henry's position as the sole ruler of the East Frankish Kingdom, ending a period of civil strife.
events.name: Henry I defeats Arnulf I in two campaigns

events.enhanced_description: In 921, Landulf I, the prince of Benevento, played a pivotal role in supporting an anti-Greek rebellion in Apulia, leading to the devastation of several Byzantine strongholds, including Ascoli. His appointment as stratego of the Theme of Longobardia by the Apulian nobility marked a significant shift in regional power dynamics, challenging Byzantine authority.
events.name: Landulf I, prince of Benevento, supports an anti-Greek Apulian rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 921, Ludmila, the Bohemian duchess and widow of Bořivoj I, was murdered by her daughter-in-law Drahomíra at Tetín. This tragic event led to Ludmila's canonization, and she became a revered figure in both the Orthodox and Catholic Churches, symbolizing the struggles within the early Bohemian nobility.
events.name: Murder of Ludmila, Bohemian duchess

events.enhanced_description: In 921, King Charles III (the Simple) and Henry I signed the Treaty of Bonn aboard a ship in the Rhine, establishing a 'pact of friendship' and recognizing the borders between their Frankish kingdoms. This treaty was a crucial step in stabilizing relations between the two rulers during a period of political fragmentation.
events.name: Treaty of Bonn

events.enhanced_description: In 921, a Hungarian mercenary force led by Dursac and Bogát successfully defeated insurgents in Brescia who were attempting to overthrow their ally, Emperor Berengar I. This victory reinforced Berengar's position and highlighted the complex alliances and conflicts within Italy during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Hungarian mercenary victory at Brescia

events.enhanced_description: In 921, a diplomatic delegation from Baghdad was sent to establish trade routes towards Bukhara, modern-day Uzbekistan. Led by Ahmad ibn Fadlan, this mission not only aimed to enhance economic ties but also facilitated cultural exchanges between the Abbasid Caliphate and Central Asian powers.
events.name: Diplomatic delegation from Baghdad

events.enhanced_description: In 921, the Battle of Sevan saw Sajid forces under Yusuf Beshir invade Armenia, besieging King Ashot II near Lake Sevan. Ashot II's counter-offensive not only repelled the invaders but also initiated efforts to restore the devastated regions of Armenia.
events.name: Battle of Sevan

events.enhanced_description: In 921, the Fatimid Caliphate achieved a decisive victory against Idrisid forces, capturing the important cities of Tlemcen and Fez. This victory solidified Fatimid control over North Africa and marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Fatimid Caliphate's victory over Idrisid forces

events.enhanced_description: In 921, the Fatimid Caliphate established a new capital, al-Mahdiya, on the Tunisian coast. This move was part of their broader strategy to consolidate power in North Africa and assert their influence over the Mediterranean.
events.name: Establishment of al-Mahdiya

events.enhanced_description: In 921, the Later Liang Dynasty reported the pacification of all 'barbarian' tribes by the Khitan Empire, marking a period of relative stability in northern China. This pacification was crucial for the consolidation of power by the Khitan and their influence over the region.
events.name: Later Liang Dynasty pacifies tribes

events.enhanced_description: In 922, Adalbert I, margrave of Ivrea, led a rebellion against King Berengar I with the support of Italian nobles. His actions prompted an invasion by Rudolph II of Upper Burgundy, culminating in Berengar's flight to Verona and Rudolph's coronation as King of Italy.
events.name: Adalbert I's rebellion against Berengar I

events.enhanced_description: In 922, Mansur al-Hallaj, a Persian mystic, was sentenced to death for heresy after a prolonged trial in Baghdad. His execution, marked by severe punishment, highlighted the tensions between mysticism and orthodoxy in the Abbasid Caliphate.
events.name: Mansur al-Hallaj's execution

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 922, the Battle of Constantinople saw Emperor Romanos I dispatch Byzantine troops to repel a Bulgarian raid. Despite initial success in storming the Bulgarian camp, the Byzantines were ultimately defeated by the main Bulgarian forces, preventing a siege of the city.
events.name: Battle of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 922, West Frankish nobles revolted against King Charles III (the Simple), leading to his deposition after a 24-year reign. He sought refuge in Lotharingia, while Robert I was crowned king, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Revolt against King Charles III

events.enhanced_description: In 923, the Battle of Fiorenzuola saw Lombard forces led by King Rudolph II and Adalbert I defeat the deposed Emperor Berengar I. This battle resulted in a pact that led to Berengar's abdication and a significant reconfiguration of power in Italy.
events.name: Battle of Fiorenzuola

events.enhanced_description: In 923, the Later Liang Dynasty fell to the Later Tang, founded by Li Cunxu, who proclaimed himself emperor and moved the capital back to Luoyang. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of China during the Five Dynasties period.
events.name: Fall of the Later Liang Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: In 923, the Qarmatians of Bahrayn captured and pillaged the city of Basra, a significant event that underscored the instability in the region and the challenges faced by the Abbasid Caliphate in maintaining control.
events.name: Qarmatians capture Basra

events.enhanced_description: In 924, the monastery of San Martín de Albelda was founded in the Kingdom of Navarre by King Sancho Garcés I and Toda Aznárez. This establishment commemorated the previous year's military successes in recapturing Nájera and Viguera, reflecting the intertwining of religious and political life in medieval Spain.
events.name: Foundation of San Martín de Albelda

events.enhanced_description: In 924, Emperor Zhuangzong of China executed General Li Jitao after discovering his continued plotting against the government. This decision highlighted the political intrigue and instability within the Later Tang Dynasty as it sought to consolidate power.
events.name: Execution of General Li Jitao

events.enhanced_description: In 924, Ahmad ibn Kayghalagh was removed from his position as the Abbasid Governor of Egypt by Caliph al-Muqtadir after a brief tenure. His replacement by Takin al-Khazari marked a significant shift in governance during a tumultuous period for the Abbasid Caliphate.
events.name: Removal of Ahmad ibn Kayghalagh

events.enhanced_description: In 924, Hungarian Magyar forces led by General Szalárd captured Pavia, the capital of the Kingdom of Italy, at the request of Holy Roman Emperor Berengar I. This event not only demonstrated the shifting allegiances in Italy but also foreshadowed further incursions into southern France by the Magyars.
events.name: Hungarian forces capture Pavia

events.enhanced_description: In 924, Holy Roman Emperor Berengar I was assassinated in Verona by one of his guards shortly after forming a new alliance with the Hungarians. This assassination allowed Rudolph II, King of Burgundy, to seize control of the Kingdom of Italy, significantly altering the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Assassination of Berengar I

events.enhanced_description: In 924, Grand Vizier Ali ibn al-Furat was removed from office by Caliph al-Muqtadir and replaced by Abdallah ibn Muhammad al-Khaqani. This change in leadership came after accusations of brutality and failure to protect pilgrims, reflecting the internal strife within the Abbasid administration.
events.name: Removal of Grand Vizier Ali ibn al-Furat

events.enhanced_description: Edward the Elder, King of the Anglo-Saxons, met his demise in battle at Farndon-Upon-Dee while combating a revolt by the Cambrians and Mercians. His death marked a significant transition in the English monarchy, leading to the ascension of his son Æthelstan as the new King of England amidst a divided support for his other son, Ælfweard.
events.name: Edward the Elder is killed in battle

events.enhanced_description: Ælfweard of Wessex, who was briefly a claimant for the English throne and favored by the Wessex nobility, died at the young age of 23, just sixteen days after the death of his father, Edward the Elder. His short-lived claim to the throne highlighted the instability and factionalism within the Anglo-Saxon succession.
events.name: Ælfweard of Wessex dies

events.enhanced_description: During the Byzantine–Bulgarian War, Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria led an assault that resulted in the burning of the Church of St. Mary of the Spring in Constantinople. This act was part of a broader conflict that underscored the tensions between the Bulgarian Empire and the Byzantine Empire.
events.name: Byzantine–Bulgarian War: Burning of the Church of St. Mary

events.enhanced_description: Following a series of raids on Constantinople, Tsar Simeon I met with Byzantine Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos at the Golden Horn to negotiate a truce. This agreement stipulated that Byzantium would pay an annual tribute to Bulgaria in exchange for the return of several cities along the Black Sea coast.
events.name: Truce arranged between Tsar Simeon I and Byzantine Emperor

events.enhanced_description: Byzantine co-Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos finalized a treaty with Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria, providing him with valuable gifts, including gold and silver shields and lances. This treaty was part of the ongoing diplomatic efforts to stabilize relations between the two empires amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Treaty concluded between Byzantine co-Emperor and Tsar Simeon I

events.enhanced_description: Stephen and Constantine Lekapenos were elevated to the rank of co-Emperors of Byzantium, joining the existing rulers Constantine VII, Romanos I, and Christopher, thus forming a pentarchy of five monarchs. This political maneuvering reflected the complexities of Byzantine imperial governance.
events.name: Promotion of Stephen and Constantine Lekapenos

events.enhanced_description: In winter, the Hungarians invaded Saxony, compelling King Henry I (the Fowler) to retreat to the Castle of Werla. Following this encounter, he negotiated a pact to pay tribute to the Hungarians for nine years, reflecting the shifting power dynamics in Central Europe.
events.name: Hungarian invasion of Saxony

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Taizu of the Liao Dynasty led a campaign to the West, reaching the former capital of the Uyghur Kingdom on the Orkhon River. This campaign marked a significant expansion of the Khitan Empire's influence in Central Asia.
events.name: Emperor Taizu's campaign to the West

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Zhuang Zong of Later Tang conferred the chancellor title upon Gao Jixing, Prince of Nanping, and established the Nanping State in Central China. This political move was part of the broader consolidation of power during the period of the Ten Kingdoms.
events.name: Creation of the Nanping State

events.enhanced_description: In March 924, a Qarmatian force attacked and destroyed returning Hajj caravans at al-Habir, capturing prominent pilgrims and leading to significant political repercussions, including the downfall of the Abbasid vizier. This incident underscored the growing power of the Qarmatians and their impact on Islamic pilgrimage traditions.
events.name: Qarmatians attack Hajj caravans

events.enhanced_description: In June 924, Fruela II ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of León and the Kingdom of Galicia following the death of his brother, King Ordoño II. His reign marked the reunification of these kingdoms, although it was marred by political tensions and his unpopular decisions among the nobility.
events.name: Fruela II becomes ruler of León and Galicia

events.enhanced_description: In August, Gyeongae ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Silla following the death of his elder brother, King Gyeongmyeong. This transition marked a continuation of the royal lineage in one of Korea's Three Kingdoms, as Silla sought to maintain its power and stability.
events.name: Gyeongae becomes the new monarch of Silla

events.enhanced_description: In the fall, during the Bulgarian–Serbian War, Tsar Simeon I dispatched a punitive expedition against Serbia, led by Theodore Sigritsa and Marmais. However, the Bulgarian forces were ambushed and defeated, marking a significant setback for Simeon I.
events.name: Bulgarian–Serbian War: Ambush of Bulgarian forces

events.enhanced_description: In November, Hamd bin Khazar, the leader of the Zenata Berber nomads, orchestrated an ambush that resulted in the death of Massala ibn Habus, the Fatimid Governor of Tahert. This event underscored the ongoing power struggles in North Africa during this period.
events.name: Ambush of Massala ibn Habus

events.enhanced_description: Nicholas I Mystikos, who served as the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople twice, passed away at the age of 73. His death marked a significant moment in the leadership of the Eastern Orthodox Church during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Death of Nicholas I Mystikos

events.enhanced_description: Stephen II was appointed as the new Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, succeeding Nicholas I Mystikos. This transition was crucial for the leadership of the Eastern Orthodox Church during a time of political and religious challenges.
events.name: Stephen II becomes Ecumenical Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: Alberic I, duke of Spoleto, attempted to seize control of Rome but was expelled by an uprising organized by Pope John X. Following his flight to Orte, he was ultimately murdered by a mob, illustrating the intense power struggles in medieval Italy.
events.name: Alberic I attempts to seize Rome

events.enhanced_description: King Rudolph II of Burgundy and his father-in-law Burchard II led an expeditionary force over the Great St. Bernard Pass to confront Hugh of Provence. Their campaign aimed to assert control over the city of Ivrea, igniting a civil conflict against Lombard partisans.
events.name: Burgundian expedition against Hugh of Provence

events.enhanced_description: Tomislav, the duke of the Croatian duchies of Pannonia and Dalmatia, was crowned as the king of Croatia. His reign was marked by an alliance with the Byzantines against the Bulgarian Empire, reflecting the geopolitical complexities of the region.
events.name: Tomislav crowned as king of Croatia

events.enhanced_description: A Fatimid expeditionary force led by Jafar ibn Obeid landed in Abruzzo, Southern Italy, and swiftly overran Apulia. Following their victory over Byzantine garrisons, they besieged the castle of Oria, resulting in a massacre of defenders and the capture of survivors.
events.name: Fatimid expeditionary force lands in Abruzzo

events.enhanced_description: In winter, Later Tang forces led by Emperor Zhuang Zong invaded Former Shu, one of the Ten Kingdoms in China, successfully incorporating it into his domains. This military action exemplified the ongoing consolidation of power by the Later Tang during this period.
events.name: Later Tang invasion of Former Shu

events.enhanced_description: A visiting Uyghur delegation inspired the development of the Khitan small script, which was based on alphabetic principles. This innovation marked a significant cultural advancement for the Khitan people.
events.name: Development of Khitan small script

events.enhanced_description: Ha-Mim declared himself a prophet and messenger of Islam among the Ghomara Berbers near Tétouan in modern Morocco. His proclamation contributed to the spread of Islam in the region during this period.
events.name: Ha-Mim proclaims himself a prophet

events.enhanced_description: In the summer, King Fruela II died after a brief reign of only 14 months, leading to the ascension of his son Alfonso Fróilaz. The subsequent revolt by nobles resulted in a division of the kingdom among several factions, highlighting the instability in the region.
events.name: Death of King Fruela II

events.enhanced_description: In the fall, John Mystikos, the chief minister of the Byzantine Empire, was deposed and exiled to a monastery. He was succeeded by Theophanes, who became a close adviser to Emperor Romanos I, amidst ongoing conflicts with Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria.
events.name: Deposition of John Mystikos

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of the Bosnian Highlands, Bulgarian forces led by Duke Alogobotur faced an ambush and defeat at the hands of King Tomislav's Croatian army. This battle marked a significant military setback for Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria in his campaigns against Croatia.
events.name: Battle of the Bosnian Highlands

events.enhanced_description: In 926, the Hungarians besieged Augsburg in Bavaria and subsequently conquered the monastery of St. Gallen in modern Switzerland. Following an unsuccessful battle with local forces, they burned the suburbs of Konstanz before defeating a Frankish army led by Duke Liutfred of Alsace.
events.name: The Hungarians besiege Augsburg in Bavaria, then conquer the monastery of St

events.enhanced_description: In 926, King Æthelstan of Wessex and Mercia successfully annexed Northumbria, compelling Wales and Strathclyde to accept his sovereignty. This marked a significant consolidation of power, as Æthelstan unified the various small kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy into what would become the Kingdom of England.
events.name: King Æthelstan of Wessex and Mercia annexes Northumbria

events.enhanced_description: In 926, Emperor Zhuang Zong was assassinated during a rebellion led by officer Guo Congqian at the Tang capital of Luoyang. His death led to the ascension of his adoptive brother Li Siyuan, who sought to establish friendly relations with the Khitan Empire.
events.name: Emperor Zhuang Zong is killed during an officer's rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 926, Emperor Taizu of the Liao Dynasty passed away after a decade of rule. He was succeeded by his son Tai Zong, while his eldest son Yelü Bei became the ruler of the Dongdan Kingdom, a puppet state of the Khitan Empire.
events.name: Emperor Taizu dies after a 10-year reign

events.enhanced_description: In 926, Pope John X formed an alliance with Hugh of Provence, which incited the wrath of Marozia, the daughter of Roman consul Theophylact I. This political maneuvering highlighted the intense power struggles within the Roman nobility.
events.name: Pope John X allies himself with Hugh of Provence

events.enhanced_description: Following the death of King Solomon, his son Rehoboam faced immediate challenges in maintaining unity among the tribes of Israel. The northern tribes seceded, establishing the separate Kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam, while Rehoboam retained control over the southern Kingdom of Judah, leading to a significant political division.
events.name: On the death of King Solomon, his son Rehoboam is unable to hold the tribes of Israel together, and the northern part secedes to become the kingdom of Israel, making Jeroboam its king

events.enhanced_description: In spring, Italian nobles revolted against King Rudolph II of Burgundy, leading to the election of Hugh of Provence as king of Italy. This shift in power dynamics was marked by the assassination of Burchard II, Rudolph's father-in-law, further destabilizing the region.
events.name: Italian nobles turn against King Rudolph II

events.enhanced_description: In 927, Simeon I, the emperor of the Bulgarian Empire, died of heart failure after a 34-year reign. He was succeeded by his son Peter I, who negotiated a peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire, reaffirming Bulgaria's territorial claims.
events.name: Simeon I of the Bulgarian Empire dies

events.enhanced_description: In 927, King Æthelstan of Wessex claimed his kingdom at Eamont Bridge, receiving the submission of High-Reeve Ealdred I of Bamburgh and likely Owain ap Dyfnwal of Strathclyde. This event solidified Æthelstan's authority and marked the unification of various Anglo-Saxon kingdoms into the Kingdom of England.
events.name: King Æthelstan of Wessex claims his kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 927, the Hungarians fought in Rome to support Margrave Peter against Pope John X. Following their involvement, they moved to southern Italy, conquering the cities of Taranto and Oria.
events.name: The Hungarians fight in Rome

events.enhanced_description: In 927, the Fatimids from Sicily, led by Sabir, captured and destroyed the city of Taranto, enslaving much of its population. This event underscored the ongoing conflicts in Southern Italy during this period.
events.name: The Fatimids capture and destroy Taranto

events.enhanced_description: In 927, Later Baekje, one of the Later Three Kingdoms of Korea, sacked the Silla capital of Gyeongju. The attack resulted in the suicide of King Gyeongae and the installation of Gyeongsun as the new ruler by the Later Baekje king Kyūn Hwūn.
events.name: Later Baekje sacks the Silla capital

events.enhanced_description: In October/November 927, the Qarmatian invasion of Iraq commenced, marking a significant military campaign in the region. This invasion would have lasting effects on the political landscape of the Middle East.
events.name: The Qarmatian invasion of Iraq begins

events.enhanced_description: In 927, the Sajid emir of Adharbayjan, Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, was defeated and captured by the Qarmatians near Kufa. This defeat illustrated the growing power of the Qarmatians in the region.
events.name: Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj is defeated and captured

events.enhanced_description: In 927, the Bulgarian Orthodox Church was officially recognized as autocephalous by the Patriarchate of Constantinople. This recognition marked a significant step in the establishment of Bulgarian ecclesiastical independence.
events.name: The Bulgarian Orthodox Church is recognised as autocephalous

events.enhanced_description: In 927, Irish preacher and abbot Cele Dabhaill mac Scannal died during his pilgrimage in Rome. His journey reflects the strong connections between Ireland and the broader Christian world during this period.
events.name: Cele Dabhaill mac Scannal dies on pilgrimage

events.enhanced_description: In 928, King Rudolph I lost the support of Herbert II, count of Vermandois, who controlled the prison where former King Charles III was held. This political maneuvering led to significant power shifts in Northern France.
events.name: King Rudolph I loses support from Herbert II

events.enhanced_description: In 928, Louis III (the Blind), former king of Provence, died in Arles after a lengthy reign, most of which he spent sightless. His death led to the ascension of his brother-in-law Hugh I, who stripped Louis's son of his inheritance.
events.name: Louis III (the Blind) dies at Arles

events.enhanced_description: In the winter of 928, King Henry I (the Fowler) subdued the Polabian Slavs along the eastern borders of his realm. He then advanced against the Hevelli tribes, capturing their capital at Brandenburg and besieging the castle at Meissen.
events.name: King Henry I (the Fowler) subdues the Polabian Slavs

events.enhanced_description: In 928, King Hywel Dda of Deheubarth undertook a pilgrimage to Rome, becoming the first Welsh ruler to do so. This journey was significant in the context of Welsh law and governance, as he began the codification of medieval Welsh law during this time.
events.name: King Hywel Dda makes a pilgrimage to Rome

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 928, a Fatimid fleet under Sabir al-Fata raided Byzantine southern Italy, capturing the locality of al-Ghiran and sacking the cities of Taranto and Otranto. The raids resulted in the enslavement of many inhabitants, reflecting the turbulent relations between the Fatimids and Byzantines.
events.name: A Fatimid fleet raids Byzantine southern Italy

events.enhanced_description: In 928, Ishanavarman II died after a brief reign of five years and was succeeded by his uncle Jayavarman IV as king of the Khmer Empire. Jayavarman IV moved the capital from Angkor to Koh Ker, marking a significant shift in the empire's political landscape.
events.name: Ishanavarman II dies and is succeeded by Jayavarman IV

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 928, Pope John X was deposed and imprisoned by Marozia, a powerful Roman senatrix, after a 14-year reign. His removal from power led to the election of Leo VI as the next pope, further entrenching the political turmoil within the papacy.
events.name: Pope John X is deposed and imprisoned

events.enhanced_description: In 928, Pope Leo VI abolished the Nin Bishopric and transferred Bishop Gregory to Skradin, effectively resolving a long-standing dispute between the Split and Nin Bishoprics within the Croatian kingdom. This decision had lasting implications for the ecclesiastical structure in the region.
events.name: Leo VI abolishes the Nin Bishopric

events.enhanced_description: In 928, Tryphon succeeded Stephen II as the patriarch of Constantinople, a position he would hold until 931. This transition was significant in the context of the Byzantine Church's influence and governance.
events.name: Tryphon succeeds Stephen II as patriarch of Constantinople

events.enhanced_description: In 929, Emir Abd al-Rahman III of Córdoba proclaimed himself caliph, establishing the Caliphate of Córdoba and breaking ties with the Fatimid and Abbasid caliphs. This declaration marked a significant moment in the history of Islamic governance in Spain.
events.name: Emir Abd al-Rahman III proclaims himself caliph

events.enhanced_description: In 929, Guy, Margrave of Tuscany and the second husband of Marozia, passed away. His death led to his brother Lambert succeeding him, further influencing the power dynamics within the region.
events.name: Guy, Margrave of Tuscany, dies

events.enhanced_description: In 929, German king Henry the Fowler led an East Frankish army to besiege the stronghold of Gana, successfully conquering it and establishing the fort of Meissen nearby. This event marked a significant military achievement in the expansion of East Frankish power.
events.name: Siege of Gana

events.enhanced_description: In 929, Henry the Fowler invaded Bohemia from the north, while Duke Arnulf I of Bavaria advanced from the south, leading to the capitulation of the Bohemians. This military campaign further solidified the influence of East Frankish rule in the region.
events.name: Henry the Fowler invades Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: In 929, the Battle of Lenzen saw Slavic forces, specifically the Redarii and Obotrites, defeated by a Saxon army near the fortified stronghold of Lenzen in modern Germany. This battle was part of the broader conflicts between Germanic and Slavic tribes.
events.name: Battle of Lenzen

events.enhanced_description: In 929, Charles the Simple, the former king of West Francia, died in prison at Péronne. His death left Rudolph II with little opposition, aside from Herbert II, Count of Vermandois, marking a significant shift in power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Death of Charles the Simple

events.enhanced_description: In 929, Mpu Sindok, the ruler of the Mataram Kingdom, relocated his court from Central Java to East Java, likely due to the eruption of Mount Merapi and threats from the Srivijaya empire. This move was pivotal in the history of the Mataram Kingdom.
events.name: Mpu Sindok moves court

events.enhanced_description: In 929, Pope Leo VI passed away in Rome after a brief seven-month reign. He was succeeded by Stephen VII, who was likely chosen by the influential Marozia from the Tusculani family, reflecting the political entanglements of the papacy.
events.name: Death of Pope Leo VI

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 929, the Slavic-Arab leader Sabir achieved a notable victory by defeating a small Byzantine fleet and seizing the coastal town of Termoli in Molise. This conquest allowed him to return to Africa with significant plunder, including slaves.
events.name: Sabir defeats Byzantine fleet

events.enhanced_description: In 930, the Althing was established at Þingvellir, marking the formation of Iceland's parliament. This assembly allowed chieftains from various tribes to gather annually to settle disputes and make collective decisions, laying the foundation for Icelandic governance.
events.name: Establishment of the Althing

events.enhanced_description: In 930, Bishopwearmouth was formed and settled in northeast England after Æthelstan granted the lands to the Bishop of Durham. This event contributed to the establishment of ecclesiastical authority in the region.
events.name: Formation of Bishopwearmouth

events.enhanced_description: In 930, Gilbert, Duke of Lorraine, besieged the city of Douai in West Francia. This military action was part of the ongoing power struggles in the region during this period.
events.name: Siege of Douai

events.enhanced_description: In 930, the Qarmatians, led by Abu Tahir al-Jannabi, sacked Mecca, desecrating the sacred Zamzam Well and carrying off the Black Stone to their homeland in Eastern Arabia. This event was a significant affront to Islamic sanctity and authority.
events.name: Sack of Mecca

events.enhanced_description: In 930, Mardavij ibn Ziyar was sent by Asfar ibn Shiruya to capture the fortress of Shamiran in Tarom. However, during the siege, Mardavij revolted against Asfar, leading to his rise as the founder of the Ziyarid Dynasty.
events.name: Mardavij ibn Ziyar's campaign

events.enhanced_description: In 930, Emperor Daigo of Japan, gravely ill, abdicated in favor of his seven-year-old son Suzaku after a 33-year reign. Daigo subsequently entered the Buddhist priesthood, while former Emperor Uda continued to wield significant influence behind the throne.
events.name: Emperor Daigo abdicates

events.enhanced_description: In 930, the independent Korean island state of Usan-guk became a protectorate of Goryeo, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of the Korean peninsula.
events.name: Usan-guk becomes protectorate

events.enhanced_description: In 930, Yelü Bei, the prince and elder brother of the Liao dynasty's Emperor Taizong, departed for China, indicating the ongoing interactions and complexities between the Liao dynasty and the Chinese states.
events.name: Yelü Bei leaves for China

events.enhanced_description: Zhou yi wang's ascension to the throne marked a significant moment in the history of the Zhou dynasty, which would go on to influence Chinese culture and governance for centuries. His reign is noted for the continuation of the feudal system and the promotion of Confucian ideals.
events.name: Zhou yi wang becomes king of the Zhou dynasty of China

events.enhanced_description: The death of King Solomon in Jerusalem marked a pivotal moment in the history of ancient Israel, leading to the division of the united monarchy into two separate kingdoms: Israel and Judah. This split had lasting implications for the political and cultural landscape of the region.
events.name: Solomon dies in Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: In 931, King Harald Fairhair, Norway's first ruler, died after a 59-year reign. He had previously divided his kingdom among his sons to maintain peace, ultimately passing power to his son Eric Bloodaxe.
events.name: Death of King Harald Fairhair

events.enhanced_description: In 931, Rollo, the first Duke of Normandy, died in Rouen after an 11-year reign. His leadership established an independent dukedom for Viking settlers, and he was succeeded by his son William I Longsword.
events.name: Death of Rollo, Duke of Normandy

events.enhanced_description: In 931, Ramiro II forced his brother Alfonso IV to abdicate and ascended as king of León in Northern Spain. His reign was marked by ruthless consolidation of power, including blinding Alfonso's sons to prevent any future claims to the throne.
events.name: Ramiro II becomes king of León

events.enhanced_description: In 931, Ramiro II expanded the borders of León eastwards, capturing Burgos and surrounding lands, which would later become known as the County of Castile. This territorial expansion was crucial for the strengthening of his kingdom.
events.name: Ramiro II expands borders

events.enhanced_description: In 931, King Morgan Hen of Glywysing and Gwent submitted to the overlordship of King Æthelstan, attending his court alongside other Welsh kings, including Hywel Dda and Idwal Foel. This event marked a significant moment in the consolidation of English influence over Wales.
events.name: Submission of King Morgan Hen

events.enhanced_description: In 931, Emir Mardavij ibn Ziyar defeated and killed his rival Asfar ibn Shiruya, swiftly conquering the Abbasid cities of Hamadan, Dinavar, and Kashan, ultimately establishing Isfahan as his capital. This victory marked the rise of the Ziyarid Dynasty in Iran.
events.name: Mardavij ibn Ziyar's victory

events.enhanced_description: In 931, the Nómine Leonesa, an important account detailing the kings of Asturias and León, was published. This work contributed to the historical understanding of the region's monarchical lineage.
events.name: Publication of Nómine Leonesa

events.enhanced_description: In March 931, Pope Stephen VII died after a three-year reign, leading to the election of John XI, who was only 20 years old. His mother, Marozia, played a significant role in the political machinations of the papacy during this time.
events.name: Death of Pope Stephen VII

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 931, Hugh of Provence ceded Lower Burgundy to Rudolph II in exchange for Rudolph's renunciation of claims to the Italian crown. This agreement solidified Rudolph's power and influence in the region.
events.name: Cession of Lower Burgundy

events.enhanced_description: In 932, Doge Orso II Participazio voluntarily retired to a monastery, signaling the decline of the Participazio family's influence over the Venetian dogeship. His departure paved the way for Pietro II Candiano to assume leadership, marking a new era in Venetian politics.
events.name: Doge Orso II Participazio retires voluntarily to a monastery, marking the end of the Participazio dominance of the Venetian dogeship

events.enhanced_description: In 932, Pietro II Candiano and Capodistria entered into a trade agreement without the necessary imperial approval, showcasing the growing autonomy of Venice. This move was met with resistance from Wintkar, who prohibited the repayment of debts to Venice, escalating tensions in the region.
events.name: Pietro II and Capodistria make a trade agreement without imperial authorization, the self-proclaimed 'Marquis' Wintkar forbids repaying any debts to Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 932, Emir Mardavij ibn Ziyar launched an invasion of Tabaristan, successfully capturing the city of Gorgan. His campaign prompted Makan ibn Kaki to seek refuge with the Samanids, where he was appointed governor of Kirman by Nasr II, highlighting the shifting power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Emir Mardavij ibn Ziyar invades Tabaristan and captures the city of Gorgan

events.enhanced_description: In 932, Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir was killed in battle against the forces led by general Mu'nis al-Muzaffar. Following his death, al-Muqtadir's brother, al-Qahir, was chosen as his successor, marking a significant moment in the Abbasid political landscape.
events.name: – Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir is killed while fighting against the forces of general Mu'nis al-Muzaffar

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 932, Alberic II led a rebellion in Rome against his stepfather, Hugh of Provence, following a personal insult at his mother's wedding. Alberic seized control of the Lateran Palace, imprisoned Marozia, and declared himself the ruler of Rome, marking a significant shift in power dynamics within the city.
events.name: Summer – Alberic II leads an uprising at Rome against his stepfather Hugh of Provence, king of Italy, after he is insulted at the wedding of his mother, Marozia

events.enhanced_description: In the summer of 932, Pope John XI was compelled to cede control of Rome to his half-brother Alberic II, who was then invested as 'Prince and Senator of all Romans.' This event marked a significant consolidation of power for Alberic and a diminishing role for the papacy in secular governance.
events.name: Summer – Pope John XI is forced to grant power over Rome to his half-brother Alberic II, who is invested as 'Prince and Senator of all Romans'

events.enhanced_description: In 933, King Henry I, known as 'the Fowler,' achieved a decisive victory against the Magyars near Merseburg after refusing to pay the annual tribute. This battle marked a turning point, as the Magyars would not raid the East Frankish Kingdom again during Henry's reign.
events.name: – Battle of Merseburg: King Henry I ('the Fowler') defeats the Magyars near Merseburg after his refusal to pay the annual tribute

events.enhanced_description: In 933, William I, known as 'Longsword,' acknowledged King Rudolph as his overlord, solidifying political ties between Normandy and the Frankish kingdom. In return, Rudolph granted William control over the Cotentin Peninsula and the Channel Islands.
events.name: William I ('Longsword'), duke of Normandy, recognizes King Rudolph as his overlord

events.enhanced_description: In 933, Prince Edwin, the youngest son of King Edward the Elder, tragically drowned while traveling to the West Frankish Kingdom. He was subsequently buried at Saint Bertin, marking a significant loss for the English royal lineage.
events.name: Prince Edwin, the youngest son of the late King Edward the Elder, is drowned en route to the West Frankish Kingdom and buried at Saint Bertin

events.enhanced_description: In 933, Fatimid forces attempted to conquer the Maghreb al-Aqsa, present-day Morocco, but faced staunch resistance from local Berber tribes allied with the Caliphate of Córdoba. This failure highlighted the challenges the Fatimids faced in expanding their influence in North Africa.
events.name: Fatimid forces fail to seize the Maghreb al-Aqsa (modern Morocco) from the local Berber tribes allied to the Spain-based Caliphate of Córdoba

events.enhanced_description: In the spring of 933, King Hugh of Provence launched a military expedition to Rome aimed at ousting Alberic II, seeking to avenge his previous humiliation. However, the campaign failed as Roman militias successfully repelled the Lombard forces, forcing Hugh to retreat.
events.name: Spring – Hugh of Provence, king of Italy, launches an expedition to Rome to remove the Roman ruler (princeps) Alberic II and avenge his humiliation (see 932)

events.enhanced_description: In 934, during the Battle of W, the combined forces of the Hungarians and Pechenegs inflicted severe casualties on the inhabitants of Constantinople and its countryside, defeating both the Byzantine Empire and Bulgaria. This victory forced Emperor Romanos I to sign a peace treaty with the Hungarians.
events.name: Battle of W

events.enhanced_description: In 934, King Henry I, known as 'the Fowler,' successfully pacified the northern territories plagued by Danish Viking raids, defeating the petty king Gnupa and conquering Hedeby. This victory helped restore stability to the region and curtailed Viking incursions.
events.name: King Henry I ('the Fowler') pacifies the territories to the north, where the Danish Vikings have been harrying the Frisians by sea

events.enhanced_description: In 934, Haakon I, known as 'the Good,' successfully reunited Norway after deposing his half-brother Eric Bloodaxe. His ascension to the throne marked a significant moment in Norwegian history, restoring stability to the kingdom.
events.name: Haakon I ('the Good'), a son of the late King Harald Fairhair, once again reunites the kingdom after he has deposed his half-brother Eric Bloodaxe

events.enhanced_description: In 934, the Eldgjá volcanic eruption occurred, marking the largest basalt flood in recorded history. This geological event had significant implications for the environment and climate of the region.
events.name: The Eldgjá volcanic eruption is the largest basalt flood in history (first documented)

events.enhanced_description: In 934, King Tewdwr of Brycheiniog attended the court of King Æthelstan, where he signed the English Land Charters. This event was significant as it united various Welsh kings, including Hywel Dda and Idwal Foel, in support of Æthelstan's campaign against King Constantine II of Scotland.
events.name: King Tewdwr of Brycheiniog attends the court of King Æthelstan and signs the English Land Charters
